reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes an Ethereum MEV bot with unusually high daily and weekly return claims and provides viewers with a deployment workflow. It directs participants to deploy the contract and fund it with Ethereum, linking larger deposits to larger trades and greater expected profit, while presenting unverified balance and profit figures as demonstration evidence.

citations.quote: Today I'll be teaching you step-by-step how to deploy an Ethereum training bot I've recently developed in the Solidity language, which can make you very easy daily passive income.
So, the next step is to fund the contract with some Ethereum to snipe liquidity pools.

You can fund the contract with whatever amount of Ethereum you want, but obviously the more you put in, the larger the transactions you will be able to sandwich and the more profit you'll be able to accumulate over time.
It takes advantage of decentralized finance platforms such as Uniswap to sandwich transactions for arbitrage!

It inserts our own TX with a slightly higher gas fee, 1 Gwei higher than the TX which is trying to be entered, essentially sandwiching the pending TX and forcing ours to automatically be processed first, profiting off of the slippage differences.

opening.argument: The presentation is accompanied by unusually explicit risk and uncertainty language, which is inconsistent with treating the outcome as assured. It says the material is not financial advice, describes cryptocurrency as highly volatile and high-risk, and expressly states that no particular outcome is guaranteed. It also acknowledges that profits vary over time and warns that gas and burn fees can waste funds. A careful viewer is therefore given material reasons to investigate independently and understand that losses are possible, rather than being promised a dependable return.

citations.quote: This content is not to be considered as financial advice, legal advice or taxation advice of any kind.
Cryptocurrency is HIGHLY volatile and a very high-risk investment.
The speaker does not guarantee any particular outcome.
The profits will fluctuate week-to-week.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account emphasizes profit figures but omits the accompanying qualifications. The material does not present those figures as guaranteed: it expressly says outcomes are not guaranteed, profits fluctuate, and operational fees can reduce funds. Showing a favorable personal result alongside clear volatility and loss warnings is not by itself proof of deceptive solicitation.

citations.quote: The speaker does not guarantee any particular outcome.
Cryptocurrency is HIGHLY volatile and a very high-risk investment.
The profits will fluctuate week-to-week.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Disclaimers do not neutralize the presentation's concrete funding instructions and prominent success claims. The speaker still tells viewers to fund a contract and says larger deposits permit larger profits, while describing substantial reported gains. A warning that outcomes are uncertain does not show that the promoted mechanism is reliable, independently verified, or safe.

citations.quote: You can fund the contract with whatever amount of Ethereum you want, but obviously the more you put in, the larger the transactions you will be able to sandwich and the more profit you'll be able to accumulate over time.
it basically took me a day to gain over half my deposit back
I've even had weeks where I made 3-6 Ethereum, sometimes more!

opening.argument: The central activity is an operational technology tutorial and demonstration. The speaker identifies the subject as teaching viewers step by step, explains Solidity and Remix, shows contract creation and compilation, and walks through deployment and wallet interaction. The supplied frames likewise show a code editor, Remix's compiler and deployment panels, a connected wallet, and blockchain-explorer pages. That makes the primary context instruction and demonstration of a smart-contract workflow, not necessarily a solicitation or certification that every result will occur.

citations.quote: Today I'll be teaching you step-by-step how to deploy an Ethereum training bot I've recently developed in the Solidity language
Remix is a web3 application that allows us to develop, compile, deploy, and launch smart contracts coded in the Solidity language.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the content instructional does not establish that it is deceptive. The described workflow concerns code, compiler settings, deployment, gas fees, and contract controls, all ordinary subjects for an operational demonstration. The speaker also explains what the functions do and shows a withdrawal function, which is consistent with teaching viewers how the tool operates rather than concealing its operation.

citations.quote: Now that our bot file is ready let's compile it
Now, you can see the four actions for our smart contract. Start, enables the bot to start sniffing out the mempool. Withdraw, stops the bot and transfers the funds back into your wallet

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial framing does not make the underlying promotion educational in a non-scam sense. It gives step-by-step deployment and funding directions, then uses claimed returns as persuasive demonstration evidence. The code interface and wallet screens show that transactions occurred, but they do not establish that the bot generated the claimed profits or that viewers would recover deposited funds.

citations.quote: Today I'll be teaching you step-by-step how to deploy an Ethereum training bot
So, the next step is to fund the contract with some Ethereum to snipe liquidity pools.
As you can see, the balance from the bot is now in my wallet.

opening.argument: The evidence shows a software and smart-contract service workflow, but does not establish several mechanisms normally associated with a scam. It does not request passwords or credentials, require recruiting a downline, or promise a fixed return. Instead, it describes transaction costs and possible burn fees, says profits fluctuate, and identifies a withdrawal action intended to return funds to the wallet. The material can therefore be understood as promotion of a technical trading tool whose results and risks require independent evaluation, without certifying that the service is safe.

citations.quote: The bot targets token contracts with max 10% burn fee and anything lower.
the contract will waste a lot of gas fees.
Withdraw, stops the bot and transfers the funds back into your wallet.
The profits will fluctuate week-to-week.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account relies on inference from a funding step rather than identifying a concealed mechanism. The material describes a deployable software contract, its start and withdrawal controls, and costs that can reduce performance. It does not show credential harvesting, recruitment, or a fixed-return guarantee. A request to fund a trading contract is not by itself proof that the transaction is fraudulent.

citations.quote: Withdraw, stops the bot and transfers the funds back into your wallet.
the contract will waste a lot of gas fees.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing mechanisms listed by the defense are not required to support this classification. The video explicitly directs viewers to deploy the contract, send it Ethereum, start it, and expect profits; it also links larger deposits to larger profit potential. A withdrawal button and fee warning do not verify that deposited funds will be returned or that the claimed returns are genuine.
